amendments.rule: Where English fuses several morphemes into one word, such as *wherein*, they share a unit **only when that shared English rendering carries the sense of every morpheme placed in it**. Reserve `added` for English that no morpheme licenses at all. This governs a fixed multi-word Hebrew expression the ASV renders with one English word too, but it never absorbs a morpheme whose sense that rendering does not carry: in `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` → *chronicles*, the two lexical nouns may share *chronicles*, while the separately segmented article takes a written *the* or is its own `unrepresented` unit; `אִם לֹא` → *surely* may share one unit when *surely* carries both morphemes' senses. Such a fused expression is headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme, rather than leaving another morpheme whose sense the rendering carries `unrepresented`. The one-English-word condition is load-bearing in both directions: `בְּיַד` → *by* and `מִפְּנֵי` → *because of* fuse, but where the ASV spends a second English word on the expression — `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses while the same idiom as *say ... nay* does not — the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. **Read that condition as one English rendering, not one English token.** A compound English preposition written in two or three words — *because of*, *by reason of*, *out of* — is a single rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and it fuses; so does an expression whose unit additionally carries a copula or other word the construction hands to the whole of it under another rule, as `לִפְנֵי` → *was before*. What defeats the condition is English the ASV spends on one morpheme in particular, so that each morpheme has a rendering of its own: `לִפְנֵי` → *to meet* gives *to* to the preposition and *meet* to `פָּנֶה`, and `עַד לְ` → *until there was* gives *until* to `עַד` and the predicate's supplied copula to the `לְ` under rule 49, while the same `עַד לְ` → *to* fuses. Test by subtraction as rules 16 and 31 do: drop the second English word and ask whether a particular morpheme has lost its rendering or only the expression as a whole is diminished. What the second morpheme is tagged does not matter; a preposition before a construct noun fuses on the same terms as a compound preposition. **And such a compound's single English word carries the preposition's own relation even where no part of it states that relation separately.** Where `מִן`, `לְ`, `בְּ` or `עַל` stands before a construct noun and the ASV writes one English preposition for the pair, the condition is met and the two share a unit headed on the construct noun: `מִפְּנֵי` → *before*, `לִפְנֵי` → *before*, `עַל־פְּנֵי` → *upon*, `בְּקֶרֶב` → *among*. **Read that list as the commonest prepositions and not as a closed one:** what licenses the fusion is that a preposition stands on a construct noun and one English rendering carries the pair, so a `כְּ`, an `אֶל`, an `אַחַר` or any other preposition in that position is read on exactly the same terms, and `כְּפִי` → *as* fuses as `לְפִי` and `מִפְּנֵי` do. Do not read this rule's first sentence as requiring a separate English trace of the ablative, directional or locative sense before fusing, and do not mark the preposition `unrepresented` beside a construct noun holding the whole word: that is the outcome the fusion sentence above forbids and the one rule 22's closing paragraph forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a word, and the subtraction test finds no second English word for either morpheme to own. **The same prohibition runs the other way, and the construct noun is the side more often mistaken.** Do not mark the construct noun `unrepresented` beside a preposition holding the whole rendering either: the noun of such a compound is not a word the ASV ever writes alone, its sense is inside the one English word exactly as the preposition's is, and the reasoning that forbids the one direction forbids the other, so the two share a unit headed on the construct noun as before. Read whether any English word in the expression renders that noun's own lexeme, which is this rule's subtraction test again: `כְּפִיךָ` → *even as* ... *art* writes nothing for `פֶּה` in particular, so the pair fuses and the suffix keeps only the *thou* rule 18 writes for it, while `לִפְנֵי` → *to meet* gives `פָּנֶה` a word of its own and rule 2 splits it. A pronominal suffix on the construct noun is no part of the fusion in either case: it takes whatever English pronoun the ASV writes for it under rule 18, or goes `unrepresented` under rule 40 where the ASV writes none, and its presence is not evidence that the preposition and its noun have separate renderings. Where the ASV instead writes a word for each — `מִפְּנֵי` → *from before*, `מִקֶּרֶב` → *from among* — each morpheme has a rendering of its own, the condition is unmet, and rule 2 splits them; what tells the two shapes apart is independently recoverable ownership under rule 2, not the raw number of English words or which senses an English preposition leaves implicit. The corpus fuses `מִפְּנֵי` to *before* in fifteen units and to *because of* in seventy-five, `לִפְנֵי` to *before* in five hundred and ninety-seven, and a preposition with `תּוֹךְ` or `קֶרֶב` to *among* in twenty-seven. Contiguity is part of the condition for such an expression: a verb and the preposition it governs, held apart by the subject or the object, is not one. It is not a condition on fusion generally — rule 35's *Nor* and *never* fuse across intervening material, because there the one English word still carries every morpheme's sense. `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded* and `הוֹסִיף ... אֶל` → *exceed* are a verb whose preposition the ASV's comparative recasting leaves unrendered, so rule 2 splits them and the preposition is `unrepresented`. Rule 22 governs a repetition of the *same* element, not the parts of an idiom. **The expression need not be an idiom, and a full lexical noun fuses on the same terms as a function morpheme.** Where Hebrew writes a generic head noun before an attributive that names the class — `אִשָּׁה` or `אִישׁ` before a participle or an adjective — and the ASV renders the pair by one English word, the two share one unit headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme: `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* is one unit headed on `זוֹנָה`, with the indefinite article going to that nominal expression under rule 15, and `אִשָּׁה` is not marked `unrepresented` beside it. The one-English-word condition and its subtraction test decide this exactly as they decide a compound preposition — dropping the English word diminishes only the expression as a whole, and no morpheme owns a part of it — so where the ASV instead spends a word on each, as `אִישׁ מִלְחָמָה` → *man of war*, the condition is unmet and rule 2 splits it. Do not read *fixed multi-word Hebrew expression* above as a requirement that the pair be idiomatic. **And a demonstrative modifying a noun is such an attributive.** Where Hebrew writes a noun with the demonstrative that modifies it — `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` and the like — and the ASV renders the pair by one English word, the two share one unit on exactly the terms just given, headed on the morpheme whose lexeme that word most directly writes, which is ordinarily the demonstrative; an article standing in the phrase takes a written *the* under rule 29 or is its own `unrepresented` unit where the ASV writes none, exactly as the article of `דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים` → *chronicles* is. `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *thus* and `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *that* both fuse, and JDG.8.1 and JDG.8.3 are the two renderings in one chapter. **And a single English word that is one morpheme's own ordinary rendering does not defeat the condition.** What defeats it is a second English word the ASV spends on one morpheme in particular, so where one word alone stands for the whole expression the pair fuses even though that word is what the ASV writes for one of the morphemes elsewhere: this is rule 40's ruling that a preposition and its noun recast as one English adverb fuse though the word is the noun's ordinary rendering, and it is this rule's own `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's*, where *harlot's* is `זוֹנָה`'s own word and `אִשָּׁה` is still not marked `unrepresented`. Do not mark the other morpheme `unrepresented` on that ground, and do not reach for rule 22's first sentence, which governs an element the ASV has left unwritten and not one whose sense stands inside a fused word. Where the ASV instead writes a word for each — `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` → *this thing* — the condition is unmet, rule 2 splits them, and each morpheme takes the word written for it. **For this rule, a particle's single idiomatic English rendering includes the pronouns the English formula requires.** The entreaty particle `נָא` → *I beseech thee* or *we pray thee* takes the complete formula, headed on *beseech* or *pray*; its English subject and object pronouns are not `added`, because they realize the particle's one entreaty rather than supply arguments of the neighbouring imperative. Where the ASV's formula omits an object, as *I pray*, align only what it writes.
amendments.why: JDG.8 analysed one and the same `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` two ways — fused at v.1, split at v.3 with `דָּבָר` marked `unrepresented` — and the verse pass that split it reached rule 22 because rule 30's generic-head-noun sentence names only 'a participle or an adjective' and stops short of a demonstrative, and because rule 30 states its 'spends on one morpheme in particular' test for a second English word without saying what to do when the single word is one morpheme's ordinary gloss. Rule 40 already answers that second question for a preposition and its noun ('Do not mark the preposition `unrepresented` on the ground that the one English word is the noun's ordinary rendering'), and this rule's own `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* is an instance of it, so the amendment widens the attributive clause to cover a demonstrative and states the ordinary-gloss ruling in the rule that owns fusion, citing rules 22, 29 and 40. Nothing in the amendment reaches a phrase the ASV writes in two English words, which is the common shape and stays split under rule 2. No corpus row shown contradicts it; the precedent tables cover the chapter's top lemmas and are silent on this pair.

Rule 40 already answers that second question for a preposition and its noun ('Do not mark the preposition `unrepresented` on the ground that the one English word is the noun's ordinary rendering'), and this rule's own `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* is an instance of it, so the amendment widens the attributive clause to cover a demonstrative and states the ordinary-gloss ruling in the rule that owns fusion, citing rules 22, 29 and 40. Nothing in the amendment reaches a phrase the ASV writes in two English words, which is the common shape and stays split under rule 2. No corpus row shown contradicts it; the precedent tables cover the chapter's top lemmas and are silent on this pair.

report: One genuine cross-verse split: `הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה` is fused into a single English word at JDG.8.1 (*thus*, noun + demonstrative, both articles unrepresented) but split at JDG.8.3 (*that* to `זֶה` alone, `דָּבָר` marked `unrepresented` under rule 22). The source is identical in both verses and nothing licenses the difference. Patched JDG.8.3 to the fused reading, headed on the demonstrative as v.1 heads it: rule 30 forbids leaving a morpheme `unrepresented` beside a single word that carries its sense, and its own `אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה` → *harlot's* example is the same shape (one English word that is the modifier's ordinary gloss, generic noun still inside the unit). Rule 22's first sentence does not reach `דָּבָר`, since nothing there is repeated or resumptive.

Direction of the fix: v.1's *thus* is nobody's dictionary word, so the fusion there is the harder reading to doubt; pulling v.3 to it is preferable to splitting v.1, which would have to hand *thus* to `זֶה` and leave a full lexical noun holding nothing.

BSB disagreements reviewed. One is a genuine error and the patch fixes it: BSB represents `דָּבָר` at JDG.8.3 (WLC.JDG.8.3.031) and the ASV alignment did not. The rest are documented convention differences, not corrections — `Td` articles for which the ASV writes no *the* (rule 29), `To` object markers (rule 16), `R` prepositions the ASV's recasting leaves nothing to say (rule 40), and the paragogic nun at JDG.8.1 (rule 32). No accepted edge was changed to move the aggregate rate.

Checked and found consistent, so left alone: waw connectives read off the ASV throughout (*And*, *Now*, *for*, *So*, *Then*, *But*, *yet*, *that*); `אֵת` H853 unrepresented against H854 *with*; `הָיָה` as copula, existential frame and possessive *had* (vv. 11, 21, 26, 27, 30, 33); article counts following how many *the*s the ASV wrote (`קוֹצֵי הַמִּדְבָּר` with two at v.7 against one at v.16); and preposition-plus-noun recastings uniformly fused (`בְּחָזְקָה` → *sharply*, `בְּרַגְלַי` → *follow*, `כָּזֹאת` → *in like manner*, `מִשָּׁם` → *thence*, `מֵעָלָיו` → *toward*, `מִלְ` → *from*, `לְבַד מִן` → *besides*, `מִסָּבִיב` → *on every side*).

The `added` units were read end to end, since the candidate table is blind to them: the three supplied coordinators (vv. 4, 20, 22) all stand where no conjunction morpheme is present, and *them* (v.25), *shekels* (v.26), *even* (v.27) and *who is* (v.35) each answer to no morpheme. No verse folds such a word into a neighbour, so there is no hidden split there.

The two large-source candidates at JDG.8.26 are both `לְבַד מִן` → *besides*; each is one rendering of which no morpheme owns a part, and they agree with each other. The verse-local ties at v.18 (*What manner of*), v.22 (three `גַּם`s against four English connectives) and v.28 (*no more*) are already named in their notes under rule 8 and were left standing.
